title: My flesh is meat indeed (John 6:51–58)
hook: the Church reads this chapter as the heart of Eucharistic faith (CCC 1336)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first great I am: I am the bread of life. Your line was bread of life. Did you pause before a first bite? Day five hundred four.

If a friend said, I am your bread, you'd take it as a metaphor. You'd nod. People say things like that. Up to now in John chapter six, the crowd could have done the same. Bread from heaven, coming to him, believing in him: it all sounds like a picture of faith. And then Jesus says something no one can comfortably take as a picture. The crowd hears it and starts arguing out loud. Today is the hardest stretch of the chapter, and for Catholics it's the center of everything they do on a Sunday.
screen: `I AM YOUR BREAD: A METAPHOR?` → `THEN HE GOES FURTHER.` → `THE CROWD ARGUES OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world." The listeners argue among themselves: how can this man give us his flesh to eat? It's the natural question. And here is the moment where a teacher would soften it if he meant it only as an image. He doesn't. He says it more strongly: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. And then: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Meat is the old word for food. Indeed means truly, really. Scholars point out that from this point John even changes verbs, from the ordinary word for eat to one often rendered chew or gnaw; how much weight to put on that is debated. The Catholic Church reads this chapter as the heart of its faith in the Eucharist. The Catechism says the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the cross would later scandalize them. Catholics believe that at Mass the bread and wine become, truly and substantially, the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine, and the Council of Trent called that change transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also hold that Christ is truly present. Many Protestant churches understand the Lord's Supper differently, some as a spiritual presence, some as a memorial. Today's line, eat, and live, is the Catholic reading in three words: whoever eats this bread will live for ever. It's why Catholics genuflect to the tabernacle, and why Sunday Mass is not optional for them. They believe they are being fed.
screen: `HOW CAN HE GIVE US HIS FLESH?` · `HE DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` · `TRULY FOOD, TRULY DRINK.` · `THE HEART OF EUCHARISTIC FAITH.` · then, large: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before the tabernacle. If you're near a Catholic church that's open, you can go in and sit near the tabernacle, the small gold box with a lamp burning beside it. If not, picture one: the candle, the quiet, the box at the front. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to say a lot. Catholics believe Christ is present there, and many simply sit with him the way you'd sit with a friend who's sick, saying nothing. If you pray, you can just stay. If you don't, sit with the quiet and the lamp. The bell holds the time.
My flesh is meat indeed. Jesus in John six: his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. Catholics read it as the Eucharist. Today's word.
screen: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: eat, and live. Today, notice what actually feeds you. And that's week seventy-two: so loved, he must increase, living water, white for harvest, made whole, bread of life, and meat indeed. Day five hundred four.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY-TWO: SO LOVED · INCREASE · WATER · HARVEST · WHOLE · BREAD · FLESH`
`DAY 504 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TO WHOM SHALL WE GO.`

howItsDone: Catholics receive Communion at Mass believing it is truly the body and blood of Christ, genuflect toward the tabernacle where the consecrated Host is kept, and many spend quiet time in adoration before it.

fork.setup: you've told a crowd your flesh is bread for the life of the world. they argue: how can he give us his flesh to eat? what do you do?
options: explain that it was only a figure of speech.
change the subject to the manna.
fork.reveal: he goes further: unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in you. for my flesh is meat indeed.

original.note: Greek: eating, chewing (John 6:54). John switches to this verb here; how strong it is, scholars debate.

trapdoor: what you thought: eat my flesh is a strong way of saying believe in me.
what it means: Catholics read it as the Eucharist, Christ truly present and truly given as food.
what a scholar hears: John shifts from phagein to trōgein in 6:54; and the Douay numbers these verses one higher than most Bibles (6:56 for 'meat indeed').
